solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Innocent overturned this necessary stuff

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped end over end, so the word is read from the other end

blocks.note: a nit is a nitwit, a simple, guileless person

explanation.surface: An innocent party has had the essentials knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: TIN is old slang for money, which British slang also calls 'the necessary'.
explanation.definitionFit: Money is what you need to get by, hence the slang 'the necessary', and tin is another slang word for cash.

clue.text: All but show frightful foul up (no zippo) as a measure of Rosy

indicators.note: all but means everything except the final letter is kept
frightful suggests a mess, so the letters of the phrase after it are thrown into a new order
no zippo says a nought is to be taken out of the letters

blocks.note: to teach someone is to show them how
taken as written
zippo is slang for nothing, a zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A dreadful mess-up described as a measure of something rosy.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosy Lee is Cockney rhyming slang for tea, so a measure of it is a cupful.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosy (Lee) means tea in rhyming slang, and a cupful of tea is the standard serving by which it is measured.

clue.text: Old Peruvian's banged up?

blocks.note: first meaning: belonging to the Incas of ancient Peru
second meaning, read as two words: in the can, slang for in prison

explanation.walkthrough: Split as IN CAN the answer is slang for locked up in jail; whole it is the adjective for the Inca people.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things of the Inca empire, and 'in can' is slang for being in prison.

clue.text: Resident could be most knowledgeable

indicators.note: could be invites a different arrangement of the word before it

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A local inhabitant might be the best-informed person around.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerd is a person with obsessive expertise, so the nerdiest is the most steeped in knowledge.

clue.text: I limit short flap on departing

definitions.note: the answer speaks in the first person: a curtailer is one who says 'I limit'

indicators.note: departing says the little word before it leaves the letters it sits in

blocks.note: curt means short, brusque
an aileron is a hinged flap on an aircraft wing
taken as written; this is what departs

explanation.surface: Someone curbs a brief panic over leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the answer's own self-description, riddle-fashion: a curtailer would say 'I limit'.
explanation.definitionFit: To curtail is to cut short or restrict, so a curtailer is someone who limits things.

clue.text: Parliamentarian devoured pancakes as part of service

definitions.note: the answer is plural: items making up a cruet service

indicators.note: something devoured is eaten up and gone, so those letters vanish from the word

blocks.note: a Scottish crumpet is a thin pancake
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician scoffed the pancakes served up at a function.
explanation.walkthrough: A crumpet is a griddle cake; in Scotland the word means a large thin pancake. Here the MP has eaten the MP out of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Cruets are the small condiment bottles of a cruet set, part of a table service.

clue.text: Line of limitation in report on credit facility

blocks.note: a return is an official report, such as a tax return
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
facility means ease, as in doing something with ease

explanation.surface: A borrowing limit set out in a statement about a credit facility.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the return crease is a line at each end of the popping crease, marking how far sideways the bowler may go.
explanation.definitionFit: The return crease is one of the white lines limiting where a cricket bowler's back foot may land.

clue.text: He had tatties mashed — yes, you've got it

indicators.note: mashed potatoes are pulped and reshaped, so the letters before it are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written; tatties are Scottish potatoes

explanation.surface: A man ate mashed potatoes, and someone confirms that's correct.
explanation.walkthrough: Tatties is Scots for potatoes; mashed is both what happened to them and the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an encouraging confirmation that someone has understood correctly, the same as saying yes, you've got it.

clue.text: Excite aged class

blocks.note: ae. is the abbreviation of Latin aetatis, aged
a rate is a class or grade, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: Stir up an elderly group of students.
explanation.definitionFit: To aerate is to charge with gas or make effervescent, and figuratively to stir up or excite.

clue.text: Like-minded, say, by temper

blocks.note: by and in can both mean by means of, as in 'by train' or 'in a car'
to temper an instrument is to tune it

explanation.surface: Of the same mind, perhaps, because of disposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temper' looks like mood but is the musician's verb, as in Bach's well-tempered clavier. 'Say' marks like-minded as one example of being in tune.
explanation.definitionFit: People in tune with each other are in agreement, sharing the same outlook.

clue.text: Messages to them informally covering troubles

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece covering another sits on top of it, so it comes first

blocks.note: 'em is the casual spoken form of them
ails means troubles, as in what ails you

explanation.surface: Notes sent to people, casually papering over their problems.
explanation.definitionFit: Emails are electronic messages, the everyday sense of the word.

clue.text: Rent is mostly excessive

indicators.note: mostly keeps most of the word but drops its last letter

blocks.note: ripe in the sense of 'a bit ripe', going too far

explanation.surface: A tenant's rent is largely over the top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid to a landlord, but it is the noun for a tear.
explanation.definitionFit: A rent is a tear in fabric, and a rip is exactly that kind of split.

clue.text: One wanting steady job never moved to weaken as before

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the following letters go missing from the word
moved says the letters are shifted about into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
to be on is to be at work, engaged in a regular job
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone after secure employment never got around to weakening, archaically.
explanation.walkthrough: The deletion is loose: ON stands for being in steady work. 'As before' marks an old word.
explanation.definitionFit: Enerve is the obsolete form of enervate, meaning to sap the strength of.

clue.text: Being a buddy of légionnaire's new name, yes

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh form of the following word

blocks.note: taken as written
I is an old spelling of aye, yes

explanation.surface: A Foreign Legion soldier's new name is affirmed by a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The légionnaire is a French soldier, flagging a French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: En ami is French for 'as a friend', so being a buddy in a French speaker's terms.

clue.text: Take to grumbling and grab opening on stage

blocks.note: to take to doing something is to start doing it
rap can mean a complaint or rebuke, and also, in Chambers, to snatch or grab

explanation.surface: Begin complaining and seize an opportunity in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is not certain: the blog read it as START + RAP, with 'grab' backing up the second piece since rap can also mean to seize.
explanation.definitionFit: A star trap is a trapdoor in a theatre stage through which an actor can spring up suddenly.

clue.text: Blighter's coming with Perrier, perhaps, Macron's present

blocks.note: a blighter or cad is a rotten fellow
Perrier is a French mineral water, eau in French

explanation.surface: A rotter arrives bearing a bottle of fizzy water as a gift for the French president.
explanation.walkthrough: Macron, the French president, signals a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadeau is the French noun for a gift, what a French speaker would call a present.

clue.text: Bullish device finally free to contain a heading in Umbrian

indicators.note: the word's ending is set free, so its last letter is dropped
a heading is what comes at the top, so only the first letter of the next word is used
to contain is to hold within, so the remaining pieces go inside

blocks.note: a trick or device is a cunning ploy
taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bullish gadget is at last free to hold the start of an Umbrian.
explanation.definitionFit: Tauric means relating to a bull, from Latin taurus, so bullish in the literal sense.

clue.text: Huge scam developing about hospital — it's crooked per Rab C

indicators.note: something developing changes shape, so the letters take a new form
about means surrounding, so the reworked letters go round the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A big fraud growing around a hospital is bent, as a Glaswegian would say.
explanation.walkthrough: Rab C. Nesbitt is a Glaswegian TV comedy character, flagging a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Camsheugh is a Scots dialect adjective for crooked or bent, so the word a Glaswegian would use.

clue.text: Who's becoming one that's done with saltpeter

blocks.note: U means upper-class, the done thing
niter (nitre) is another name for saltpetre

explanation.surface: A riddle asking which person ends up as one who handles saltpetre.
explanation.walkthrough: U, from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, marks what is socially acceptable, the done thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A uniter brings things together, making separate parts become one.

clue.text: Uncertainty beginning to emerge in flimsy addition to mast

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which alone is taken
in places the preceding pieces inside the word that follows

blocks.note: frail means flimsy, easily broken
an if is an uncertainty, as in ifs and buts
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Doubt starts to surface over a flimsy extension to a ship's mast.
explanation.definitionFit: A fife rail is a rail fitted round a ship's mast, holding belaying pins for the rigging.

clue.text: Wage slave may show this display, I seem disturbed

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: to present is to display
taken as written

explanation.surface: A downtrodden worker admits to looking upset.
explanation.definitionFit: Presenteeism is staying at work longer than needed, or while ill, to look committed, typical of an overworked employee.

clue.text: Fantastic, first fetch will include special section's celebrations?

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or wildly altered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
S is short for special
S is short for section

explanation.surface: A first catch is described as fantastic, with a special bit added.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a Festschrift celebrates by way of a book, not a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A Festschrift is a volume of essays published to honour a scholar, a celebration in print.

clue.text: Solvent which would be flowing if female opened it

indicators.note: the clue imagines a different opening letter, so the answer's first letter is the one swapped out

blocks.note: fluent means flowing, as in fluent speech
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A liquid that would run freely if a woman opened it.
explanation.walkthrough: This works backwards: put F at the front of the answer in place of its E and you get a word for flowing.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry an eluent is the solvent used to wash substances through a chromatography column.

clue.text: Son expressed concern over popular fraud

indicators.note: expressed here means pressed out, squeezed from the word
in a down entry over means placed above, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: a stake is a concern or interest in a business
S is the abbreviation for son
in means fashionable, popular

explanation.surface: A boy voiced his worry about a widespread swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expressed' reads as spoke but is squeezed out, as juice is expressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A take-in is a deception or swindle, a noun from to take in, to fool someone.

clue.text: Piano features in Blondie song about having a backbone

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the song title is read from its end
features in means appears inside, so the letter is placed within the word

blocks.note: Denis was a 1978 Blondie hit
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft

explanation.surface: A piano part appears in a Blondie track about spinal courage.
explanation.walkthrough: Blondie's 1978 hit was Denis; the title runs backwards and the P slips in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Spined means having a spine, so literally having a backbone.

clue.text: I am lad picking up tip in Daily Express, as it was

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its first letter, the only one taken
picking up means taking aboard, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: I'm is short for I am
a lad is a boy
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A boy reports picking up a tip from a tabloid newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Express is a British tabloid; here Express is the verb. 'As it was' marks an old spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Imbody is an obsolete spelling of embody, to give concrete form to, express.

clue.text: English music mag's hot for Net

blocks.note: E is short for English
the NME (New Musical Express) is a British music paper
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A British music magazine's hot pick is the Internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net' looks like the Internet, but it is the verb to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: To net something is to catch it in a mesh, and to enmesh is likewise to entangle.

clue.text: Splendid person holding up article forming body of law

indicators.note: in a down entry up means read from bottom to top, so the word turns round

blocks.note: a sun is a person of great brilliance
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A grand figure supports a clause that makes up a legal code.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sunna is the body of Islamic custom and practice based on Muhammad's example, used as a basis of law.

clue.text: Pike taking in mostly catty publican for Private Frazer?

indicators.note: taking in means admitting inside, so one piece goes within the other
mostly keeps all but the final letter

blocks.note: a luce is a fully grown pike
a catty is a Chinese weight, and kin is the Japanese equivalent

explanation.surface: A Dad's Army scene: Pike and a spiteful barkeeper, for Frazer.
explanation.walkthrough: Pike and Frazer are both privates in the BBC sitcom Dad's Army; Frazer is the Scot, so the answer is a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Luckie is Scots for an elderly woman, especially an alewife, the woman who keeps a tavern.

clue.text: I mark mixture, as we say, to stain

indicators.note: as we say points to how the word is spoken, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: taken as written
M is short for mark, the old German currency
a brew is a mixture

explanation.surface: I note down a recipe to dye things.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbrue is to stain or soak, especially with blood.

clue.text: Bit of puff going into adjunct's love song?

indicators.note: going into means entering, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: Serene is the word added to Highness in a prince's title
an ad is a piece of publicity, puff

explanation.surface: A short piece of breath goes into an accompaniment for a love song.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'His Serene Highness' the word Serene is an adjunct to the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A serenade is music sung or played at night under a lover's window, so a love song; the question mark marks it as typical, not the only kind.

clue.text: Some, as usual, loitering with intent, eg, in county lacking greens?

indicators.note: some means a portion, so the answer is a part of the following words
lacking means without, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: letters running across the two words
Sussex is a county in southern England
greens is old slang for sex

explanation.surface: Some suspicious lingering in a county without much green space.
explanation.walkthrough: Two routes to one answer: the letters run inside 'as usual', and Sussex minus its last three gives them again. The sus law let police stop people for loitering with intent.
explanation.definitionFit: Sus is British slang for suspicion of loitering with intent, the offence under the old sus laws.

clue.text: Free the Beeb before leaving

indicators.note: leaving says the letter before it goes out of the word

blocks.note: Auntie is a nickname for the BBC, also called the Beeb
a is short for ante, Latin for before

explanation.surface: Release the BBC before it goes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beeb and Auntie are both British nicknames for the BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something that is tied up is to untie it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: The process of advancing without using Latin's desinence

indicators.note: without using means leaving out, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: advancing money is lending it
L is short for Latin

explanation.surface: A grammar note: going forward without Latin's word endings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advancing' looks like moving forward; it is the moneylender's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Desinence is the grammarian's word for an ending or inflectional suffix of a word.

clue.text: Suffer simple RSM's shriek?

blocks.note: to stand something is to put up with it
easy means simple

explanation.surface: Put up with a plain sergeant major's yell.
explanation.walkthrough: An RSM is a regimental sergeant major, famed for bellowed parade-ground commands.
explanation.definitionFit: Stand easy is the drill command telling soldiers to relax, the kind of order an RSM shouts.

clue.text: English note found going back through autograph album

indicators.note: found means discovered inside, so the answer is lurking in the words that follow
going back means read right to left

blocks.note: letters spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: An English musical note discovered in an autograph book.
explanation.definitionFit: Lah is the British spelling of la, the sixth note of the tonic sol-fa scale.
